dervis-irab:18-42.t:
* Vocabulary:
(غُلْباً) plural of أغلب, like حمر as the plural of أحمر and حمراء. One says: حديقة غلباء, i.e. a garden of thick trees, with its plots densely intertwined. So the gardens are ones with thick trees; it is a majāz mursal (metonymic trope), like المرسن (an animal's nose-place, used for a human nose), in the sense of "thick" in general. There is also a figurative usage in the attribution (isnād), because the gardens themselves are not thick; rather, their trees are thick. Al-Zamakhsharī's wording is:
"It may be that each garden is made غلباء, meaning their density and the abundance and size of their trees, as you say: 'a huge garden'; or that its trees are made غلب, i.e. huge and thick. The original use of the description غلب is for necks, and it was then borrowed. ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib said:
يمشي بها غلب الرقاب كأنهم ... بزل كسّين من الكحيل جلالا
(Thick-necked ones walk in it, as though they were nine-year-old camels clothed in tar as caparisons.)"
One says أسد أغلب, i.e. a lion with a thick neck; القلب [Translator's note: so in the source; presumably الغلب] is its plural; it was then borrowed for anything thick. البزل is the plural of بازل, used for male and female camels when the tooth has broken through, which happens in the ninth year; الكحيل is tar; and الجلال is the plural of جلّ (a caparison). He is describing a desert in which thick-necked lions walk, as though they were young camels smeared with tar until it lay upon them like caparisons. So كسين is an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra muṣarraḥa) and الجلال is a tarshīḥ (a reinforcing detail of the metaphor). It is also narrated as كأنهم, by borrowing the pronoun of rational beings for others.
In al-Asās and al-Lisān, the gist is: "بينهما غلاب, i.e. a contest for mastery between them; تغالبوا على البلد (they contended for the land); غلبته على الشيء: I took it from him, and he is مغلوب عليه (overpowered for it). أيغلب أحدكم أن يصاحب الناس معروفا means: is any of you unable…? 'He is a free man and he has refused — shall we then overpower him against himself?', i.e. shall we compel him? شاعر مغلّب: one who was often overcome, or one who was judged the victor — so it is both blame and praise. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
فإنك لم يفخر عليك كعاجز ... ضعيف ولم يغلبك مغلّب
(No weak, helpless man has boasted over you, nor has one often overcome overcome you.)
Among the figurative usages: هضبة غلباء (a massive hill), عزة غلباء (overpowering might), اغلولب العشب (the grass grew thick), and حدائق غلبا."
(أَبًّا) In al-Miṣbāḥ: "الأبّ is the pasture which people have not sown, of what beasts and grazing livestock eat." It seems to be taken from أبّه when one heads for it, because it is sought out and travelled to for grazing, or from أبّ لكذا when one gets ready for something, because it is ready for grazing. Al-Zamakhsharī's wording: "الأب is pasture, because it is يؤبّ, i.e. sought and travelled to for grazing; الأب and الأم are brothers [in meaning]. He said:
جذمنا قيس ونجد دارنا ... ولنا الأبّ به والمكرع
(Our root is Qays, Najd is our home, and ours in it are the pasture and the watering-place.)"
الجذم, with kasra and sometimes fatḥa, is the root from which something else is cut off. الأب and الأم, with fatḥa and doubling, mean pasture, because it is يؤبّ and يؤمّ, i.e. sought out. المكرع is the watering-place. He says: we are of the tribe of Qays, Najd is our home, and ours in it, i.e. in Najd, are the pasture and the place of drinking; it contains self-praise for nobility and courage.
It has been said that the Companions — who were the people of the Hijaz and the owners of the language in which the Quran was revealed — did not understand some of the rare words in the verses of the Book. Of this is what Abū ʿUbayd reported in al-Faḍāʾil from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī: that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq was asked about the saying of the Exalted «وفاكهة وأبا» and said: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I said about the Book of Allah what I do not know?" It is transmitted from Anas that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb recited on the pulpit «وفاكهة وأبا» and said: "This fruit we know; so what is الأب?" Then he turned back upon himself and said: "This, indeed, is affectation, O ʿUmar." In one narration: then he threw down a staff that was in his hand and said: "This, by the life of Allah, is affectation; and what harm is it to you, O son of ʿUmar's mother, not to know what الأبّ is?" Then he said: "Follow what has become clear to you of this Book, and what has not, leave it." Al-Zamakhsharī commented on ʿUmar's words with an excellent comment, which we cite below:
"If you say: this resembles a prohibition of pursuing the meanings of the Quran and investigating its difficulties, I say: he did not mean that. Rather, those people's greatest concern was devoted to action, and occupying oneself with any knowledge that is not acted upon was affectation in their view. He meant that the verse is set out to remind man of the favour of his food and to call forth his gratitude, and it is known from the purport of the verse that الأب is part of what Allah has caused to grow for man as provision for him and his livestock. So hold to what is more important: rising to give thanks to Allah for what has become clear to you and was not obscure of the favours He enumerated, and do not let yourself be distracted from it by seeking the meaning of الأبّ and knowing the particular plant of which it is the name. Be content with the general knowledge until it becomes clear to you at another time. Then he advised people to proceed on this course in similar difficulties of the Quran."
How did the exegesis of the Quran begin?
To complete this important discussion, we see fit to present this subject in some detail because of its full connection with the method we have followed in this book. The fact is that the Quran occupied many groups of people for a period of time: the people of faith were occupied with it, and the people of disbelief pursued it, each from the angle of his concern. Quranic studies and exegesis first began in the time of the Messenger ﷺ. In his era we see a Bedouin asking him about the meaning of some words of the Quran, as in the saying of the Exalted «ولم يلبسوا إيمانهم بظلم», saying: "And which of us has not wronged himself?" The Prophet ﷺ explained it as shirk (associating partners with Allah) and cited as evidence for it the saying of the Exalted: «إن الشرك لظلم عظيم». Many ḥadīths connected with the exegesis of the Quran are narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the books of ḥadīth such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others; some of them are limited to mentioning its merits and explaining some of its verses with a brief explanation that shows the legislative point or the admonition in the verse. It is narrated from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There will come on the Day of Resurrection a huge, fat man who will not weigh with Allah as much as the wing of a gnat. Recite, if you wish: فلا نقيم لهم يوم القيامة وزنا." However, not everything that has come in ḥadīth on exegesis may be given consideration. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal — in the third century AH — says: "Three things have no basis: exegesis, the battle-prophecies (al-malāḥim) and the campaigns (al-maghāzī)." Perhaps he meant the exegesis in which people mixed sound and unsound ḥadīth, which was the subject of give-and-take and of many people's statements in his age.
Moreover, the Companions took two positions in early Islam. Some were scrupulous about speaking on the Quran; among them were Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar and others, and ʿAbd Allāh used to reproach Ibn ʿAbbās for interpreting the Quran by poetry. The second group were those who were not scrupulous and interpreted the Quran according to what they understood from the Messenger, or according to their own understanding by comparison with Arabic poetry and the speech of the Arabs. Among them were ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and those who took from them. Ibn ʿAbbās stood at the head of the exegetes by opinion who took the poetry of the Arabs as a means of uncovering the meanings of the Quran, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib used to praise Ibn ʿAbbās and say: "It is as though he looks at the unseen through a thin veil."
In al-Mubarrad's al-Kāmil and Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī's al-Aghānī: ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa, while a youth, came in to Ibn ʿAbbās, who had with him Nāfiʿ ibn al-Arzaq [Translator's note: the source has الأرزق here and الأزرق below; the name is Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq]. Ibn ʿAbbās said to him: "Will you not recite to us something of your poetry, O son of my brother?" So he recited to him:
أمن آل نعم أنت غاد فمبكر ... غداة غد أوم رائح فمهجر
(Is it from the family of Nuʿm that you are setting out early tomorrow morning, or going in the evening, or at midday?) [Translator's note: أوم in the source is presumably أم.]
until he completed it — and it is eighty verses. Al-Azraq said to him: "By Allah, Ibn ʿAbbās! We drive the camels hard to come to you and ask you about religion, and a youth of Quraysh comes to you reciting folly to you and you listen to him?" He said: "By Allah, I did not hear folly." He said: "Did he not recite to you:
رأت رجلا أما إذا الشمس عارضت ... فيخزى وأما بالعشي فيخسر
(She saw a man who, when the sun faces him, is disgraced, and in the evening is ruined)?"
He said: "That is not what he said. He only said: فيضحى وأما بالعشي فيخصر (he is exposed to the sun, and in the evening he is cold)." He said: "Do you memorize what he said?" He said: "By Allah, I have heard it only this very hour." Then he recited it from its beginning to its end. It was said to him: "We have never seen anyone with a better memory for transmission than you." He said: "I have never heard anything and forgotten it; and I hear the voice of the wailing woman and block my ears, disliking to memorize what she says." Then it happened that Nāfiʿ asked Ibn ʿAbbās about the saying of the Exalted «لا تظمأ فيها ولا تضحى». He said: "You will not sweat in it from the intensity of the sun's heat." He said: "And do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the poet's word فيضحى?" Among the Companions who followed this approach were Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and others, and they were followed by al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, al-Suddī and others.
(الصَّاخَّةُ) In al-Mukhtār: "الصاخة is the cry that deafens by its intensity. You say صخ الصوت, of the pattern ردّ; and from it the Resurrection was named الصاخة." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "صخ لحديثه is like أصاخ له (he listened attentively to it); so the Blast was described as الصاخة figuratively, because people listen attentively to it." Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī said: "الصاخة is that which bequeaths deafness, while it makes one hear; and this is of the marvels of eloquence, like his saying:
أصمّهم سرّهم أيام فرقتهم ... فهل سمعتم بسر يورث الصمما
(Their secret deafened them in the days of their parting — have you ever heard of a secret that bequeaths deafness?)
and the saying of Abū Tammām:
أصم بك الناعي وإن كان اسمعا ... وأصبح مغنى الجود بعدك بلقعا
(The announcer of your death deafened [us] with you, though he made [us] hear; and the abode of generosity after you has become a barren waste.)"
By the life of Allah, the cry of the Resurrection makes one hear: it deafens to this world and makes one hear the matters of the Hereafter.
(تَرْهَقُها) In al-Mukhtār: "رهقه: it covered him, of the pattern طرب; and from it is the saying of the Exalted: ولا يرهق وجوههم قتر ولا ذلّة; and in the ḥadīth: 'When one of you prays towards something, let him يرهقه,' i.e. let him come close to it and not be far from it."
(قَتَرَةٌ) a blackness like smoke; you see nothing more dreadful than the combination of dust and blackness on the face.

* I'rab:
(مِنْ أَيِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ مِنْ نُطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ) a resumptive clause set out to begin explaining what He bestowed on him, after the emphatic description of him as ungrateful for the favours of his Creator. (من أيّ شيء) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) (خلقه). The interrogative is for affirmation (taqrīr) together with belittlement; some exegetes combined the two and said: "Here the interrogative is for affirming the belittlement." (من نطفة) is a badal (substitute) with repetition of the preposition from his saying (من أي شيء خلقه). The fāʾ is for sequence in mention, and (قدّره) is a past verb, its fāʿil (agent) a latent (mustatir) pronoun, optionally, its implied form being "huwa", and a mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
(ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ ثُمَّ أَماتَهُ فَأَقْبَرَهُ ثُمَّ إِذا شاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ) (ثم) is a conjunction for sequence with delay. (السبيل) is accusative by ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb) with an implied verb, its implied form being "ثم يسّر السبيل يسّره"; the definiteness conveys generality. The clause (يسّره) is explicative. Al-Samīn's wording: "His saying ثم السبيل يسّره: the pronoun may refer to man, with السبيل an adverb, i.e. He made easy for man the way, i.e. the way of good or evil, like His saying وهديناه النجدين. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: it may also be accusative as the second object of يسّره, with the hāʾ referring to man, i.e. He made him ready for the way, i.e. He guided him to it. I say: then it must be made to include (taḍmīn) the meaning of أعطى so that it governs two accusatives, or the preposition is omitted, i.e. He made him ready for the way, i.e. guided him to it." What follows is conjoined to it. He said (فأقبره) and did not say فقبره, because القابر is the one who buries with his hand, while المقبر is Allah the Exalted. One says: قبر الميت when he buries him with his own hand, and أقبره when he orders another to put him in a grave. The object of the willing is omitted, the implied form being "when He wills his raising".
(كَلَّا لَمَّا يَقْضِ ما أَمَرَهُ) (كلا) is a rebuke and a restraint for man, who persists in his blindness, deluded by his delusion, overreaching in arrogance through his self-admiration. (لما) is a jussive particle of negation, and (يقض) is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by (لما), the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter. It is made jussive by (لما) to indicate that self-admiration and pride have not ceased to cling to man up to the very hour he is in. (ما) is a mafʿūl bihi, and the clause (أمره) is its ṣila (relative clause), with the referring pronoun omitted, i.e. به.
(فَلْيَنْظُرِ الْإِنْسانُ إِلى طَعامِهِ) resumptive speech set out to begin enumerating the successive favours upon man. The lām is the lām of command, (ينظر) is an imperfect verb in the jussive by the lām of command, (الإنسان) is its fāʿil, and (إلى طعامه) is attached to (ينظر).
(أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْماءَ صَبًّا) (أنّا) with fatḥa on the hamza; it and what follows are an interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun) in the position of the genitive as a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) from (طعامه). The meaning is that pouring the water is a cause of bringing out the food, so it includes it. It was also read with kasra on the hamza, as a resumption explaining how the food is brought about. (أنّ) and its noun; the clause (صببنا) is a verb and its fāʿil, (الماء) is the mafʿūl bihi, and (صبا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْأَرْضَ شَقًّا) conjoined to the preceding clause and parsed like it. The secret of attributing the splitting to Him, the Exalted, will come in the section on rhetoric.
(فَأَنْبَتْنا فِيها حَبًّا وَعِنَباً وَقَضْباً وَزَيْتُوناً وَنَخْلًا وَحَدائِقَ غُلْباً وَفاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا) The fāʾ is a conjunction, (أنبتنا) is a verb and its fāʿil, (فيها) is attached to (أنبتنا), (حبا) is a mafʿūl bihi, and what follows is conjoined to it. القضب and القضبة are fresh fodder (al-raṭba).
(مَتاعاً لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعامِكُمْ) (متاعا) is a maṣdar confirming (أنبتنا), because His causing things to grow is a provision for all living beings; or it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), the governor being omitted, its implied form being "He did that as a provision for you". (لكم) is attached to (متاعا), and (لأنعامكم) is conjoined to (لكم).
(فَإِذا جاءَتِ الصَّاخَّةُ يَوْمَ يَفِرُّ الْمَرْءُ مِنْ أَخِيهِ وَأُمِّهِ وَأَبِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ وَبَنِيهِ لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنْهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ) The fāʾ is resumptive, and the speech is resumptive, set out to begin explaining their states on the Day of Return. You may also make the fāʾ a conjunction, with the speech conjoined, so as to order what follows it after what preceded it of abundant favours and successive blessings. (إذا) is a future adverb containing the meaning of condition, attached to the omitted apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) understood from His saying (لكل امرئ), the implied form being "each one will be preoccupied with himself". The clause (جاءت) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation to it, and (الصاخة) is its fāʿil. (يوم) is a badal from (إذا), i.e. the day he flees in it; the clause (يفرّ) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation to it, (المرء) is its fāʿil, (من أخيه) is attached to (يفر), and what follows is conjoined to (أخيه). (لكل امرئ) is a fronted khabar (predicate), (منهم) is a naʿt (adjective) of (امرئ), and (يومئذ) is an adverb annexed to its like, attached to (يغنيه) [Translator's note: the source prints يفنيه, a misprint for يغنيه]; the tanwīn is a substitute, i.e. on the day when these many things take place. (شأن) is a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), and the clause (يغنيه) is a naʿt of (شأن).
(وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُسْفِرَةٌ ضاحِكَةٌ مُسْتَبْشِرَةٌ) (وجوه) is a mubtadaʾ; what licenses beginning with it although it is indefinite is the division into kinds (al-tanwīʿ). (يومئذ) is an adverb annexed to its like, attached to (مسفرة), and the tanwīn is a substitute for a clause. (مسفرة) is the khabar of (وجوه), and (ضاحكة) and (مستبشرة) are two further khabars of (وجوه).
(وَوُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْها غَبَرَةٌ تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ) The wāw is a conjunction, (وجوه) is a mubtadaʾ, and (يومئذ) is an adverb annexed to its like, attached to (ترهقها). (عليها) is a fronted khabar and (غبرة) a postponed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the khabar of (وجوه). The clause (ترهقها قترة) is a second khabar of (وجوه): (ترهقها) is an imperfect verb with a fronted mafʿūl bihi, and (قترة) is a postponed mubtadaʾ. [Translator's note: so in the source; (قترة) is in fact the fāʿil of (ترهقها).]
(أُولئِكَ هُمُ الْكَفَرَةُ الْفَجَرَةُ) (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ; (هم) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl) or a second mubtadaʾ; (الكفرة) and (الفجرة) are two khabars of (أولئك) or of (هم), and [in the latter case] the clause is the khabar of (أولئك).

* Rhetoric:
Figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī) in His saying (ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْأَرْضَ شَقًّا): it is a figurative attribution, for the Exalted attributed the splitting to Himself by way of attributing the act to the cause. It has been said that the attribution is literal and that the claim of its figurativeness is one of the doctrines of the Muʿtazila. But al-Bayḍāwī himself follows al-Zamakhsharī in the figurativeness of the attribution, saying: "He attributed the splitting to Himself, the Exalted, as the attribution of the act to the cause." The truth lies with al-Zamakhsharī in this, for its figurativeness does not mean that the acts of servants are created by them, because an act is attributed literally only to the one in whom it subsists, not to the one who brought it into existence; so objecting to it is arbitrary.
